title: Question 2(b): Extended Comparison (25 marks)
content_html:
Question 2(b): Extended Comparison (25 marks)

Used for: Component 1, Section A — comparing a set product with an unseen resource

What This Question Looks Like

This is the single largest question on the first paper. You are given an unseen resource and asked to compare it with a set product in the same media form, focusing on representation. You will have a copy of both in front of you. This is an extended response, so it needs a clear structure and a sustained comparative argument from start to finish.

Key Fact

25 marks out of the paper’s 45 in Section A. Comparative connectives such as ‘whereas’, ‘similarly’ and ‘in contrast’ must run through every paragraph, not just the introduction and conclusion.

What a Strong Response Does

  • Interweaves both products in every paragraph — never a block on one, then a block on the other.
  • Focuses on representation — how each product constructs a person, group, place or issue.
  • Uses named, precise evidence from both texts — not vague general impressions.
  • Reaches a comparative conclusion — a final judgement about how the two products are similar and different overall.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Read the unseen resource carefully — Annotate it as closely as the set product you already know well.
  2. 2
    Choose three comparison points — For example, how each represents gender, how each uses image, how each addresses its audience.
  3. 3
    Plan pairs, not lists — For each point, note one piece of evidence from the set product and one from the unseen resource side by side.
  4. 4
    Open with a comparative thesis — State how the two products are similar and/or different in their overall approach to representation.
  5. 5
    Write each paragraph as a single comparison — Introduce the point, give evidence from product one, pivot with ‘whereas’ or ‘similarly’, then give evidence from product two.
  6. 6
    Conclude with a direct comparative judgement — Answer the question by stating clearly which product represents its subject more conventionally, or how their approaches differ overall.

Timing

Read + plan
5 min Write
20 min Check
3 min

Around 28 minutes for 25 marks. This is worth spending your longest planning time on, since a weak plan usually produces two separate blocks instead of a true comparison.

Compare how women are represented in this unseen film poster and The Man with the Golden Gun poster.

Interwoven comparison, not two blocks

In The Man with the Golden Gun poster, women are represented as passive and decorative, positioned around Bond in swimwear with their bodies angled towards him, constructing them as objects of the male gaze. In contrast, the unseen poster foregrounds its female lead in an active pose at the centre of the composition, holding a weapon rather than being held, which constructs a far more empowered representation for a modern audience.

Second point, still comparative

Similarly, both posters use tagline text to frame their female characters, but whereas the 1974 tagline emphasises Bond’s conquests, the unseen tagline foregrounds the heroine’s own mission, suggesting changing social attitudes towards gender roles across the decades separating the two products.

Why this works: Both products appear in every paragraph, comparative connectives drive the structure, and the comparison builds towards a clear judgement about changing representation.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Two separate essays — One paragraph entirely on the set product, then one entirely on the unseen resource, never brought together.
  • ✗
    Connectives only in the introduction — ‘Whereas’ and ‘similarly’ need to appear throughout, inside paragraphs, not just to open the answer.
  • ✗
    Ignoring the unseen resource’s detail — Some students focus almost entirely on the familiar set product because it feels safer. Give both equal, precise attention.
  • ✗
    No final judgement — Trailing off after the last example instead of stating a clear overall comparative conclusion.

title: Question 2(a): Explaining Context (5 marks)
content_html:
Question 2(a): Explaining Context (5 marks)

Used for: Component 1, Section A — context of production on one set product

What This Question Looks Like

Question 2(a) asks you to explain the context of production in relation to one set product, in a different media form from Question 1. It is worth only 5 marks, so the exam board expects a short, sharply focused answer — not an essay on the historical period.

Key Fact

5 marks means roughly 5–7 minutes. A tight answer that links context directly to one or two specific features of the product beats a long, general account of the period every time.

What a Strong Response Does

  • Names the context precisely — the decade, social attitude, event or industry factor relevant to the product.
  • Points to a specific feature of the product — an image, a headline, a slogan.
  • Joins the two explicitly — shows how the context explains why that feature looks the way it does.
  • Stays brief — two or three tight sentences, not a page of background.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Identify the context type — Is the question pointing you towards social, historical, cultural, political or industry context?
  2. 2
    Pick one clear fact — Choose a single, accurate piece of contextual knowledge you are confident about.
  3. 3
    Find the feature it explains — Locate one detail in the product that this context directly accounts for.
  4. 4
    Write cause, then effect — “Because [context], the product [does this].” Keep the sentence structure this simple.
  5. 5
    Stop — Resist the urge to add unrelated background facts. One well-explained link is worth more than three loose ones.

Timing

Choose context
1 min Write
4 min Check
1 min

Around 6 minutes total. This is the shortest question on the paper — do not let it overrun into Question 2(b)’s time.

Explain the context of production of this advertisement.

Context named, then tied to one feature

The 1956 Quality Street advertisement was produced during a period of post-war social conservatism, when advertising commonly depicted idealised, traditional family roles. This is reflected in the advert’s illustration of a well-dressed family gathered together at Christmas, which reflects mid-1950s expectations of domestic harmony and traditional gender roles rather than any more modern, diverse representation of family life.

Why this works: One precise context point, one specific feature, and a direct sentence joining the two — all within a tight length appropriate to 5 marks.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Context as an add-on — Describing the period, then separately describing the product, with the two never actually connected.
  • ✗
    Writing too much — This is a 5-mark question. A long answer wastes time needed for Question 2(b).
  • ✗
    Vague context — “Things were different back then” is not a context point. Name the specific social or historical detail.
  • ✗
    Analysing media language instead — This question wants context, not a close analysis of camera angles or colour choices.

title: Exam Technique
content_html:
Exam Technique Guides

Step-by-step guides for every GCSE Media Studies question type. Learn the method, study a model answer on a named set product, and avoid the common mistakes that cost marks.

Component 1: Exploring the Media

Question 1: Media Language (15 marks)

Analyse media language in one set print product. Stepped question building to a top-tariff analysis part. Reference to context may be needed.

Question 2(a): Explaining Context (5 marks)

A short, focused answer linking context of production directly to a specific feature of one set product.

Question 2(b): Extended Comparison (25 marks)

Compare a set product with an unseen resource in the same media form. The biggest single question on the paper.

Questions 3 & 4: Industries and Audiences (35 marks)

Two stepped questions moving from short recall parts to longer explanation, covering industries and audiences across two forms.

Component 2: Understanding Media Forms and Products

Question 1: Television Extract (20 marks)

Two-part question on a screened extract: analyse media language or representation, then make judgements and draw conclusions.

Question 2: Television Industries/Audiences/Contexts (10 marks)

Moves away from the extract to test knowledge of industries, audiences or contexts for your set television option.

Questions 3 & 4: Music Video and Online Media (30 marks)

A single extended judgement on media language or representation, plus a shorter question on industries, audiences or context.

title: Questions 3 & 4: Industries and Audiences (35 marks)
content_html:
Questions 3 & 4: Industries and Audiences (35 marks)

Used for: Component 1, Section B — stepped questions on media industries and audiences

What This Question Looks Like

Section B uses two stepped questions on two different media forms from film, newspapers, radio and video games. Question 3 assesses media industries in relation to one form; Question 4 assesses industries, audiences or media contexts in relation to a different form. Each stepped question moves from short, low-tariff recall parts towards longer parts requiring explanation and application to the set product.

Key Fact

Section B is worth 35 marks in total, split across the two stepped questions. Because either question can cover industries, audiences or context, you must revise all three areas for every Section B form you study.

What a Strong Response Does

  • Uses the set product as evidence for an industry or audience point — not as something to analyse for its own sake.
  • Matches the length of the answer to the marks available — short parts get short, precise answers; longer parts need developed explanation.
  • Applies theory to a named product — for example, Uses and Gratifications theory applied to a specific set product, not just listed.
  • Covers ownership, funding, regulation, targeting or audience response as relevant to the question.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Check the marks for each part — A stepped question shows its structure clearly; let the marks guide how much you write.
  2. 2
    Answer early parts directly — Low-tariff parts often reward accurate recall: name the owner, the regulator, the release platform.
  3. 3
    Build the final part into an explained argument — Use connectives like ‘this means’ and ‘as a result’ to show consequence, not just fact.
  4. 4
    If using Uses and Gratifications, name the need and apply it — State which of the four needs (information, personal identity, integration and social interaction, entertainment) and explain how the named product meets it.
  5. 5
    Keep content and industry/audience focus separate — Only mention layout, colour or camerawork if it directly illustrates an industry or audience point, such as branding across platforms.
  6. 6
    Finish the final part with a clear statement — Answer the specific question asked, rather than trailing into general facts about the industry.

Timing

Read parts
2 min Write both questions
34 min Check
3 min

Around 39 minutes for both stepped questions combined. Spend roughly proportional time to the marks on offer in each part — do not spend as long on a 2-mark opener as on an 8-mark final part.

Explain how Desert Island Discs satisfies audience needs, using Uses and Gratifications theory.

Named need applied to the product, not just listed

Uses and Gratifications theory argues audiences actively choose media to satisfy specific needs. Desert Island Discs satisfies the need for personal identity: listeners hear well-known guests reflect honestly on formative life experiences and choose music that has shaped them, which can prompt listeners to reflect on their own values and life story. This active, reflective use of the programme goes beyond simple entertainment and explains part of its long-running appeal to a loyal audience.

Why this works: Names the theory, selects one specific need, and explains exactly how the named product meets it rather than listing all four needs generically.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Listing all four Uses and Gratifications needs with no application — Naming the theory is not enough; apply one need to the named product.
  • ✗
    Analysing content instead of industry or audience — Describing a website’s colour scheme only helps if it illustrates a branding or targeting point.
  • ✗
    Mismatched length — Writing a full paragraph for a 2-mark opening part wastes time needed for the higher-tariff final part.
  • ✗
    Vague ownership or funding claims — “It is owned by a big company” is too vague; name the specific owner, funding model or regulator where you know it.

title: Question 1: Media Language (15 marks)
content_html:
Question 1: Media Language (15 marks)

Used for: Component 1, Section A — media language on one set print product

What This Question Looks Like

You are given a copy of one set product — for example a magazine cover, a film poster, a newspaper front page or a print advertisement — and asked to analyse its media language. The question is stepped: earlier, lower-tariff parts may ask you to identify or explain features, before the final and biggest part asks you to analyse how media language constructs meaning. Reference to relevant contexts may also be required.

Key Fact

This question is worth 15 marks out of Section A’s 45. The command word in the final part is ‘analyse’, not ‘describe’ — an answer that only names techniques cannot reach the top bands.

What a Strong Response Does

  • Names precise techniques — camera angle, typography, colour palette, mode of address — using accurate terminology.
  • Explains connotation, not just presence — what does the feature suggest, and why was it chosen?
  • Links every point to meaning for the target audience — who is this designed to appeal to, and how?
  • Uses context where relevant — historical, social or industry context that shaped the choice.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Scan the whole product first — Look at image, layout, colour, typography and language before you write anything. Note the target audience.
  2. 2
    Underline three or four strong features — Choose features you can say something precise about, not just anything you notice.
  3. 3
    For each feature, add a ‘because’ — “This uses a close-up shot because it creates intimacy and makes the celebrity feel accessible to the reader.”
  4. 4
    Build to a point about the whole product — How do the features work together to construct one overall meaning or representation?
  5. 5
    Add context only if it strengthens the point — A one-sentence link to when or why the product was made, tied to a specific feature.
  6. 6
    Finish on the audience — End by stating clearly what impression the product leaves on its intended audience.

Timing

Scan + underline
2 min Write
13 min Check
2 min

Roughly 17 minutes for 15 marks within the 90-minute paper. Do not spend so long describing the image that you run out of time to explain effect and meaning.

Analyse how media language is used to construct meaning on this magazine cover.

Feature named, then effect explained

The Vogue cover uses a medium close-up of the model with direct mode of address, her gaze meeting the reader’s eye-line. This constructs a sense of intimacy and confidence, positioning the reader as being spoken to directly rather than observed from a distance. The high-fashion styling and bold masthead placement work together to reinforce Vogue’s established brand identity as an aspirational, high-status magazine.

Audience link to close

These choices target Vogue’s core readership of fashion-conscious adults who use the magazine to access an aspirational lifestyle, constructing the cover as both a fashion statement and an invitation to consume that identity.

Why this works: Precise terminology, a clear ‘because’ for every feature, and a closing link to the target audience rather than a list of features.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Feature-spotting — Listing colour, font and image with no explanation of effect. Always add why the choice was made and what it suggests.
  • ✗
    Describing instead of analysing — “There is a close-up of the model” is description. “The close-up connotes intimacy” is analysis.
  • ✗
    Context as a history lesson — Only use context when it is tied to a specific feature of the product, not as a general fact dropped in.
  • ✗
    Forgetting the audience — Every strong analysis paragraph should end by connecting back to who the product is for.

title: Questions 3 & 4: Music Video and Online Media (30 marks)
content_html:
Questions 3 & 4: Music Video and Online Media (30 marks)

Used for: Component 2, Section B — music video, artist websites and online/social media

What This Question Looks Like

Question 3 (20 marks) asks you to make judgements and draw conclusions through analysis of your set music products — the music video and the artist’s online, social and participatory media — focusing on either media language or representation. Unlike the television question, it is a single extended response, not split into parts. Question 4 (10 marks) tests media industries, audiences or media contexts connected to the music topic.

Key Fact

Section B is worth 30 marks in total. Question 3 needs a full structure from the first sentence — an opening line of argument, developed points with named examples, and a conclusion — because there is no part (a)/(b) scaffold to guide you.

What a Strong Response Does

  • States a clear line of argument early — not just a topic, but a position on the question.
  • Uses named, specific examples from the music video and/or online media, not general impressions.
  • Applies Uses and Gratifications precisely when relevant to Question 4 — naming one need and applying it to the actual set product.
  • Links industry and audience where relevant — for example, how streaming and social media change how artists reach fans.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Identify whether the question is on media language or representation — This decides which examples from the video and website you select.
  2. 2
    Plan a three-point structure — Each point should combine a named technique or representation with a judgement about its effect.
  3. 3
    Open with your line of argument — State your overall judgement in the first or second sentence, using the question wording.
  4. 4
    Develop with balanced argument — If discussing stereotypes, consider both how they aid quick understanding and how they may reinforce a narrow view.
  5. 5
    Conclude directly — Return explicitly to the question and state your final judgement.
  6. 6
    For Question 4, apply theory to the named product — Do not simply list the four Uses and Gratifications needs; explain how the specific product satisfies one of them.

Timing

Plan Q3
4 min Write Q3
16 min Write Q4
12 min

Around 32 minutes for both questions combined. Because Question 3 has no part (a)/(b) scaffold, spend a few extra minutes planning its structure before you start writing.

To what extent does the music video construct an authentic representation of the artist?

Line of argument, then named evidence and judgement

The video constructs a largely authentic representation of Stormzy by grounding him visually in recognisable South London settings, using long tracking shots through familiar streets rather than the polished studio sets typical of many mainstream pop videos. This is highly effective in reinforcing his established brand identity as a grime artist rooted in a specific community, though the highly stylised lighting in the video’s final sequence arguably shifts towards a more constructed, aspirational image, suggesting the representation is not purely observational but carefully crafted for commercial appeal.

Why this works: Opens with a clear judgement, supports it with a precisely named technique, then complicates the argument rather than settling for a single, one-sided claim.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    No structure from the start — Because Question 3 is not split into parts, some answers drift without an opening line of argument. Plan the whole shape before writing.
  • ✗
    Listing the four Uses and Gratifications needs — Naming them without applying one to the actual set product will not reach the higher bands.
  • ✗
    One-sided stereotype arguments — Treating every stereotype as simply harmful, rather than weighing its role in fast, familiar communication too.
  • ✗
    Context bolted onto the end — Add a sentence like “this reflects the time it was made” without ever explaining the specific link; always tie context directly to a technique or representation.

title: Question 1: Television Extract (20 marks)
content_html:
Question 1: Television Extract (20 marks)

Used for: Component 2, Section A — the screened extract question

What This Question Looks Like

You watch a roughly three-minute extract from your set television programme, played twice with a six-minute gap for notes in between. Question 1 is in two parts and focuses on either media language or representation in that extract — never both at once. Part (a) asks you to analyse the extract; part (b) asks you to make judgements and draw conclusions. Reference to relevant contexts may be required.

Key Fact

You get two minutes to read the Section A questions before the extract is shown. Use this time to know exactly what to look for — media language or representation — before you watch.

What a Strong Response Does

  • Names precise techniques — a specific camera shot, edit or piece of mise-en-scène, not vague description.
  • Explains how techniques create meaning in part (a), before moving to judgement in part (b).
  • Takes a position in part (b) — is this typical of the genre, or does it challenge convention? Is the technique highly effective, or only partially?
  • Ends with a substantiated conclusion that ties every point back to one central argument.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Use the two-minute reading time — Check whether the question is on media language or representation, so you know exactly what to watch for.
  2. 2
    During the first viewing, note key moments — Jot down timings or brief cues for camera shots, editing, dialogue and mise-en-scène.
  3. 4
    Use the six-minute gap to plan — Turn rough notes into two or three precisely worded points, each with a named technique.
  4. 5
    Watch again to confirm and add detail — Check your points are accurate and add one further precise example if you can.
  5. 6
    Write part (a) as analysis — Name the technique and explain how it creates meaning, using precise vocabulary throughout.
  6. 7
    Write part (b) as judgement — State a clear position, support it with evidence, then close with a conclusion that answers the question directly.

Timing

Read questions
2 min Watch + note
~12 min Write parts (a) and (b)
~28 min

The extract viewing is fixed at around 12 minutes including the note-taking gap. That leaves roughly 28 minutes to write both parts — aim for slightly longer on part (b), since judgement answers need room to build an argument.

(b) To what extent does the extract present a typical representation of masculinity?

Judgement, not description

The extract largely presents a typical representation of British-Muslim masculinity found across the sitcom, but it also complicates it. Mobeen is shown taking on a caring, protective role towards his sister, shot in a static mid-shot that lingers on his concerned expression rather than cutting away quickly, which slows the comedic pace and signals sincerity. This is only partially conventional: while the caring-brother figure is a familiar sitcom archetype, the extract’s refusal to undercut the moment with an immediate joke arguably challenges genre expectations that comedy must interrupt sentiment.

Why this works: Takes a clear position (“largely typical but also complicates it”), supports it with a precisely named technique, and reaches a substantiated judgement rather than simply describing the scene.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Retelling the plot — Describing what happens in the extract instead of analysing how techniques construct meaning.
  • ✗
    Vague technique description — “The camera moves around” scores far lower than “a low-angle shot positions the character as powerful.”
  • ✗
    No judgement in part (b) — Listing more examples without ever stating whether something is typical, effective or significant.
  • ✗
    Treating stereotypes as one-sided — A stronger answer considers both how a stereotype aids quick understanding and how it may reinforce a narrow view.

title: Question 2: Television Industries/Audiences/Contexts (10 marks)
content_html:
Question 2: Television Industries, Audiences or Contexts (10 marks)

Used for: Component 2, Section A — the non-extract television question

What This Question Looks Like

Question 2 moves away from the screened extract entirely. It tests your knowledge and understanding of media industries, audiences or media contexts connected to your set television option — for example, how a broadcaster and funding model shaped production, or how the programme targets and is consumed by its intended audience.

Key Fact

Worth 10 marks out of Section A’s 30. Unlike Question 1, this question can be answered without referring back to the extract you watched — it draws on your wider study of the set television option.

What a Strong Response Does

  • Answers the exact focus set — industries, audiences or context, not a mixture of unrelated facts.
  • Uses specific, accurate detail — the broadcaster, scheduling slot, funding model or regulatory body, named precisely.
  • Explains consequence — how a production or industry fact shaped what the audience actually sees.
  • Links areas together where useful — for example, how funding shapes representation, or how scheduling shapes audience reach.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Identify the focus word — Is the question asking about industries, audiences, or context specifically? Answer only that.
  2. 2
    Recall two or three precise facts — About the broadcaster, funding, scheduling, regulation or target audience of your set option.
  3. 3
    Turn each fact into an explained point — State the fact, then explain its effect on production or on the audience.
  4. 4
    Consider linking areas — A joined-up answer connecting industry decisions to audience reach or representation often scores more highly.
  5. 5
    Close with a direct answer — Make sure your final sentence responds explicitly to the question wording.

Timing

Plan
2 min Write
9 min Check
2 min

Around 13 minutes for 10 marks. Keep it proportionate — this is a shorter question than Question 1, so two or three well-explained points are enough.

Explain how scheduling has shaped the audience for Trigger Point.

Fact, then explained consequence

Trigger Point was scheduled in a peak-time evening slot on a mainstream terrestrial channel, aimed at reaching the broadest possible mass audience rather than a niche one. This scheduling decision shapes the programme itself: tense cliffhangers are built to encourage audiences to stay tuned across the advert break, and the crime drama’s accessible, fast-paced narrative style suits viewers watching as part of a shared family evening rather than a specialist genre audience actively seeking out crime drama.

Why this works: Names a specific industry fact, then explains its direct consequence for both production choices and audience reach, rather than stopping at description.

Common Mistakes

  • ✗
    Referring back to the extract’s content — This question wants industry, audience or context knowledge, not further analysis of camera shots.
  • ✗
    Mixing all three areas vaguely — Answer the specific focus the question asks for rather than covering industries, audiences and context all at once.
  • ✗
    Stating facts with no consequence — Naming a broadcaster or funding model is only the start; explain what it leads to.
  • ✗
    Overwriting — This is a 10-mark question; two or three well-explained points are enough, so keep answers proportionate.
